newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Palme murder probe boss suspended over tax claim.
newsitem.headline: Palme murder probe boss suspended over tax claim.

text.p: The detective in charge of the fruitless 11-year-long investigation into the assassination of Swedish Prime Minister Olof Palme was taken off the inquiry on Tuesday over allegations that he was a tax dodger.

Hans Olvebro, head of a probe that has been dogged by mistakes and scandals, was suspended from the Palme case over allegations that he had failed to declare to tax authorities that he was using a service car privately.
"We have not yet discussed what he will be assigned to. We'll do that next week," said Swedish police chief Lars Nylen.
Olvebro received formal notice on Tuesday that he had been accused by state prosecutors of tax evasion totalling 100,000 Swedish crowns ($14,000) over a two-year period.
Public prosecutor Tomas Lindstrand told reporters Olvebro would probably be called in for police questioning next week.
Tax authorities said last year they were investigating Olvebro, who has acknowledged that he used his service car privately and that police had paid the rent for his apartment in Stockholm.

Olvebro said he did not regard the benefits as taxable and that a former police chief had approved his private use of the car. He said he had been forced to use the car because of threats to his family's life related to the Palme investigation.
The Palme investigation team, which numbered more than 300 detectives at its peak, has dwindled to a handful of officers sifting through evidence to try to find fresh leads.
Palme, a controversial left-winger, was walking home from a central Stockholm cinema in 1986 with his wife Lisbet when he was gunned down from point blank range by a lone assassin.
Neither the man nor his weapon has ever been found and the police investigation suffered from major errors from the very beginning.
The investigation started badly when police failed to find the bullets used in the murder and passers-by were left to pick them up from the street and hand them in.

Two police chiefs, a public prosecutor and a justice minister have lost their jobs as a result of the investigation into the killing and three government commissions into the police handling of the case have been set up.
Olvebro said in 1994 that he expected the case to be cleared up before the end of that year.
Christer Pettersen, cleared of the murder when the case against him collapsed, regularly features on front pages of Swedish newspapers as the man police are convinced carried out the murder.

Last year investigators spent a month in South Africa after allegations by apartheid-era police spies that a South African hitman killed Palme because of his anti-apartheid views. ($1=6.965 Swedish Crown)
